# `cap_grant`: `main` performs IO but its grant is empty

The program performs IO (here, printing), but `main`'s grant is empty. A
program is granted exactly what `main` requests: its `needs` clause together
with any `Cap(P)` parameters, or, when it has neither, the module's `needs`
line. A `main` bounded by `needs ()` therefore requests nothing, so any IO
reached from it is an error. (A `main` with no clause, no `Cap` parameter and
no module `needs` line is granted nothing too; that case is reported with the
missing `needs` line, as `cap_needs`.)

## A program that triggers it

```march
mod Main do
  needs IO.Console

  fn main() needs () do
    println("hello")
  end
end
```

## The fix

Name in `main`'s `needs` clause the capability the program actually uses. The
compiler's `help:` line names it, and `forge fix` rewrites the clause. Dropping
the clause also works here, because `main` then requests the module's `needs`
line; the clause documents (and bounds) what the program can do.

```march
mod Main do
  needs IO.Console

  fn main() needs IO.Console do
    println("hello")
  end
end
```

## Why the rule exists

The grant on `main` is a ceiling on the whole program: a dependency that
tries to open a socket in a program granted only `IO.Console` is rejected at
compile time. That only means something if a program with no grant really
can do nothing, so undeclared IO is an error rather than an implicit `needs IO`.

See also: [the language reference](../capabilities.md).
